scenes.narration: The genes do not care about Coraline; they care about copies. Coraline () is a 2002 British fantasy horror children's novella by author Neil Gaiman. Gaiman started writing Coraline in 1990, and it was published in 2002 by Bloomsbury and HarperCollins.

Take away the meaning and Coraline still functions — that is the disturbing part. It was awarded the 2003 Hugo Award for Best Novella, the 2003 Nebula Award for Best Novella, and the 2002 Bram Stoker Award for Best Work for Young Readers. The Guardian ranked Coraline #82 in its list of 100 Best Books of the 21st Century.

The unconscious does not argue with Coraline; it simply acts first. It was adapted as a 2009 stop-motion animated film, directed by Henry Selick under the same name. A young girl named Coraline Jones and her parents move into an old house that has been divided into flats.

Coraline feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. The other tenants include former actresses, April Spink and Miriam Forcible, and Mr. Bobo (commonly referred as the "Crazy Old Man Upstairs"), who claims to be training a mouse circus.

The bleak reading of Coraline is also the most testable one. The flat beside Coraline's, which lies behind a big brown door, remains empty. During a rainy day, she discovers the locked door in the living room, which has been blocked by bricks.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Coraline. Bobo relays her a message from the mice warning her against going through the door. Spink and Forcible read Coraline's fortune on tea leaves and agree that she is in danger before giving her a lucky adder stone that is "good for bad things".

The self that experiences Coraline is a committee, not a king. Despite these warnings, Coraline decides to unlock the door when she is home by herself the day after, finding the brick wall behind the door gone. In its place is a long passageway, which leads to a flat identical to her own, inhabited by her Other Mother and Other Father, button-eyed and exaggerated doppelgängers of her parents.

Reproduction explains more of Coraline than any philosophy dares to admit. In this "Other World", Coraline finds everything to be better than her own – the Other Parents are attentive, her toy box is filled with sentient toys, the world's counterpart of Mr. Bobo trains rats, and the world's counterparts of Spink and Forcible perform a cabaret show in their flat.

Once you see Coraline as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. She even finds the feral black cat that wanders around the house in the real world can talk; however, she learns he is not of the Other World; he only travels from one world. The Other Mother offers Coraline a chance to stay in the Other World forever, if Coraline will allow buttons to be sewn over her eyes.

The story Coraline tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. Upon her return to her flat, Coraline finds her real parents are missing, eventually discovering that the Other Mother has kidnapped them. Though frightened of returning, Coraline goes back to the Other World to confront the Other Mother and rescue her parents.

Meaning is not found in Coraline — it is manufactured for it. As she ponders this situation in the front yard, the Cat advises Coraline to challenge the Other Mother, as "her kind of thing loves games and challenges". The Other Mother tries to convince Coraline to stay, but she refuses and is detained behind a mirror as a punishment.

The cold light on Coraline leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. In the darkness, she meets a trio of ghost children, each from a different era, who had allowed the Other Mother, truthfully an evil being known as "The Beldam", to lure them into her world and sew buttons over their eyes. The ghost children recount how she eventually stopped loving them and cast their spirits aside.

Coraline did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. They implore Coraline to avoid their fate and to help find the essences of their souls so that they can finally escape the Other World and move on to the afterlife. After the Beldam releases Coraline from the mirror, Coraline proposes a game in which she must find the essences of the ghost children's souls and her parents, which are hidden throughout the Other World.

The honest version of Coraline starts by giving up the comforting part. If Coraline wins, she, her parents and the ghost children may go free; if not, Coraline will stay and finally accept the Beldam's offer of having buttons sewn over her eyes. Coraline goes through the Other World and overcomes all the Beldam's obstacles, using her wits and the adder stone to locate the souls' essences.

Strip Coraline of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. At the close of the game, the ghost children warn her that even if Coraline wins, the Beldam will not let them go. Having deduced her parents are imprisoned in a snow globe nearby, Coraline tricks the Beldam by saying her parents are behind the door in the drawing room.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Coraline shows exactly where that breaks. As the sorceress opens the door, Coraline throws the cat at her, grabs the snow globe, and she and the cat escape to the real world with the key. In doing so, she forces the door shut on one of the Beldam's hands, amputating it.

What looks like free choice in Coraline is older than choice itself. Back in her home, Coraline finds her parents safe and have mysteriously forgotten about their capture. That night, Coraline has a dream in which she meets the ghost children before they are allowed to finally rest in peace.

Nobody designed the part of Coraline you experience — it was inherited. They warn her that her task is still not done as the Beldam's amputated hand is in the real world, attempting to steal the key needed to unlock the door that connects the two worlds. Coraline goes to an old and bottomless well in the woods by her house, luring the hand there with the key and casting both down the well.

Every serious account of Coraline eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. Coraline returns home, victorious, and prepares to go about the ordinary life she has come to accept and love. Coraline is often irritated by rain, her "crazy" grown-up neighbours and not being taken seriously because of her young age.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Coraline — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. She is very busy most of the time and sometimes inattentive, but she loves and cares about her daughter. The Cat is a black cat from the real world, who acts as a mentor to Coraline and guides her through her journey.

The selfish-gene reading of Coraline makes it less romantic and far more precise. He is unnamed, as he explains that cats do not need names to tell each other apart, but the Beldam refers to him as "Vermin". He has a sarcastic personality, constantly belittling Coraline, but befriends her and helps her escape from the Beldam.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. He is defiant of the sorceress, but trembles at the thought of being stuck in the Other World forever. The Beldam alias The Other Mother is the main antagonist of the novel.

The feeling that Coraline means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. Jones but taller and thinner, with long black hair that seems to move by itself, black button eyes, paper-white skin and extremely long and twitchy fingers with long and dark red nails. During the course of the novel, she becomes taller, thinner and paler, having little physical similarities to Mrs.

Nothing in Coraline was built for you — it was built for reproduction. She cannot create, but only copy, twist and change things from the real world when constructing her version of it. She collects children by luring them into her world and love bombing them before eventually convincing them to let her sew buttons into their eyes, which allows her to then consume their lives and hold their souls as prisoners after their deaths.

The psychology underneath Coraline is simpler and older than the story on top. The Other Father is one of the creations of the Beldam, in the image of Mr. The Other Father is used to help trick Coraline to stay in the Other World.

Behind Coraline sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. Like her real father, he has a study and sits there during the day and will not talk to Coraline for long. He does not work, he merely occupies the study and is not permitted to talk to Coraline without the Beldam's influence.

The nihilist does not deny Coraline — he only refuses to flatter it. He appears to be much more enjoyable than Coraline's real father and always tries to be cheerful and fun in front of Coraline. The Beldam ends up punishing him for revealing too much to Coraline by transfiguring him into a soft, doughy and grub-like creature and orders the Other Father to trap Coraline so she cannot win her challenge.

What culture calls destiny in Coraline is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. April Spink and Miriam Forcible are a pair of retired actresses who live in the flat under Coraline's. They own many aging Scotties and talk in theater jargon, often referencing their glory days as actresses.

The genes do not care about Coraline; they care about copies. In the Other World, they are youthful and perform continuously in front of anthropomorphic dogs. Later in the novel, the Other Spink and Forcible appear to be conjoined twins inside a cocoon-like sac where they possess the second soul.

Bobo is a retired circus performer living in the flat above Coraline's and is commonly referred to throughout the story as the "Crazy Old Man". Over the course of the book, he claims to be training mice to perform in a mouse circus, and often brings Coraline messages from them.

One of the girls has blonde hair with a circle of glittering silver, a dress with a pattern of spider webs and a pair of silver butterfly wings coming out of her back (implying that she might be a fairy). They were trapped by the Beldam at different times before Coraline and reside in the dark space behind the mirror.

The bleak reading of Coraline is also the most testable one. After having their souls restored, they are allowed to enter the afterlife. Gaiman has acknowledged Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland and "The New Mother" by Lucy Clifford as major influences on the novella.
